courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Tagged pointers: a version counter beside the pointer
md: Tagged pointer = pointer plus a counter compared and swapped as one unit, bumped on every successful CAS. It turns "same value" into "same value and same version".

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Per-query deltas, paired tests and confidence intervals
md: Queries are not the only noise source. If a stage is trained, its score also varies with the random seed. Use the same seeds and checkpoints for every stage you are not ablating, and when the ablated stage itself is retrained, run several seeds and report the spread, or a seed-to-seed swing can masquerade as a component effect.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Sequential vs random ids, and why random ids are not authorization
md: Parler's public posts were meant to be readable one at a time. Sequential ids plus no rate limit turned "anyone can read a post" into "anyone can copy the entire site, with GPS locations". Authorization decides who may read an object; rate limits and unpredictable ids decide how cheaply someone can read all of them. You need both.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: What Active Directory is: one directory for thousands of machines
md: A domain is not a wall. Domains in one forest trust each other automatically, and the Enterprise Admins group of the forest root is an administrator in every domain (next lesson). Plan protection for the whole forest, not one domain at a time.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AS-REP roasting and password spraying against AD
md: Turning off pre-authentication hands out crackable material to anyone; 4768 with pre-auth type 0 finds it. Spraying hides under per-account lockout; count distinct accounts per source in 4771 and 4776, not failures per account.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Tiered administration, Protected Users and LAPS
md: Tiering fails quietly through agents. A backup, monitoring or patching tool that runs as SYSTEM on DCs, managed from a Tier 1 console, makes that console Tier 0. List everything installed on DCs and everyone who controls it.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Format string bugs as read and write primitives
md: A format string bug is a primitive factory: the read directives leak, and %n writes. The cure is structural and cheap: constant format strings, enforced by -Werror=format-security and static analysis.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: OPSEC through the defender's eyes: every action leaves a trace
md: Map each emulated step to the log that must record it before the exercise. If the step passes unseen, the gap is in one of three places: the data was never collected, it was collected but no rule looked, or a rule fired and nobody acted. Lesson 12 names these gaps.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: Outcome grading is not the same as correct behavior. A grader only sees what it checks: tests that cover one interpretation, a database diff, an answer string. Anything outside the check (rudeness, a policy step skipped, an unrelated file deleted) can pass silently.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Keeping the context window under control
md: Compaction is lossy. The Agent SDK docs warn that specific instructions from early in the conversation may not survive a summary. Put durable rules in a file that is re-injected on every request (the SDK uses CLAUDE.md for this), not only in the first user message.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Evaluating memory and the ways it fails
md: Memory is untrusted input that outlives the session. Record provenance on every write (user said it, a tool returned it, the model inferred it), only promote user-stated facts to instructions-like status, show retrieved memories to the model as quoted data, and give users a way to view and delete what the agent remembers.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Reward design: hidden tests, partial credit and judges
md: Partial credit is not automatically better. A reward that counts tests which already passed pays the agent for the starting state, so on hard tasks the policy can learn that touching nothing beats trying. Credit only the change you want, and make breaking existing behavior cost something.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: EchoLeak: one email, zero clicks, Copilot leaks
md: Every one of Microsoft's controls existed and every one had a gap. Layered defence only works if each layer is complete on its own: all Markdown syntaxes, all allowlisted domains, all retrieval paths.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Misinformation and unbounded consumption
md: Agents multiply consumption: one user request can trigger many model calls and tool calls in a loop. Cap steps per task and total tokens per task, not only per request, or a confused agent (or an injected one) can run until the budget is gone.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
md: A generator's novelty number is only as good as its reference set and structure matcher. Note that the same disorder issue from the GNoME critique appears here: the synthesized TaCr2O6 was disordered, and MatterGen's ordered-disordered matcher exists so that an ordered variant of a known disordered compound is not counted as new.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: What an allocation trace records and why you would replay it
md: Live bytes are not RSS. RSS counts whole pages the process has touched, including allocator metadata, rounding and free holes. The gap between the two is the overhead you are usually hunting.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
md: scikit-learn's LocalOutlierFactor has two modes. With novelty=False (the default) only fit_predict and negative_outlier_factor_ exist. With novelty=True you get predict, decision_function and score_samples, but the docs warn to call them only on new data: scoring the training points that way gives wrong results, and predict will not match fit_predict.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: API keys, bearer tokens and session cookies
md: An API key in a mobile app or a web page is public. Anyone can unpack the app and read it. Keys that must stay secret belong on servers; a client that runs on the user's device needs a per-user token instead. Defender view: a fixed prefix like `sk_` lets secret scanners find leaked keys in code; log the key id (never the secret) per request and revoke on any leak.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Scopes, consent phishing and refresh token rotation
md: Changing the password does not reliably remove an app's granted consent. RFC 9700 only says servers *may* revoke refresh tokens on a password change, and the consent record itself stays. Response to consent phishing means finding and revoking the app's consent and tokens, not just resetting credentials.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: GraphQL risks: introspection, batching and query depth
md: In GraphQL one request can mean one operation or thousands. Price requests by the work they ask for, check authorization where each field is resolved, and let the server, not the client, decide what is too expensive.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: How static analysis finds bugs: taint from source to sink
md: Source, propagation, sanitiser, sink. A finding is a path from a source to a sink with no sanitiser on it. False positives come from checks the tool cannot understand; false negatives come from sources, sinks or paths it does not model.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Prioritising with CVSS, EPSS and KEV, computed on real CVEs
md: KEV says "exploited now", EPSS says "likely soon", CVSS says "how bad if it happens", and your inventory says "where, how exposed, how important". Rank by evidence of exploitation and exposure first, severity second.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 1: analysis, then redo that repeats history
md: Redo is decided per page by LSN comparison alone, never by whether the transaction committed. Updates 80 and 100 belong to losers and are redone anyway. After redo the database is exactly as it was at the crash, and only then does undo begin.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Testing input types on your own data
md: Never assume the input type is right because results look plausible. Measure the grid of query and document settings on your own labeled queries, and keep tests that fail loudly when a call site or the index metadata drifts.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Inside Tokio's scheduler: local queues, stealing, LIFO slot
md: Tokio guarantees fairness only in a weak sense: if the number of tasks is bounded and no task blocks, every woken task is eventually scheduled. It does **not** promise round-robin order. Two ready tasks A and B may see A scheduled five times before B, even if A calls `yield_now`, a future that returns `Pending` once after arranging its own wakeup, so the scheduler may run something else first.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
md: Clip length does not map to patches by simple division. YAMNet needs at least 0.975 s of audio (0.96 s plus the rest of the last 25 ms STFT window), pads anything shorter with silence, and rounds longer audio up to a whole hop. Our script gets 1 patch for 0.5 s, **2 patches for 1.0 s**, 10 for 5 s and 20 for 10 s.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Storing passwords wrong: plaintext, encryption, fast hashes
md: Hashing is not encryption. If a company can email you your old password, it is stored in plaintext or reversibly encrypted. A hash with no salt is only slightly better than plaintext against an attacker with a list of common passwords.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Kinds of MFA, and the maths inside a TOTP code
md: A TOTP code proves you hold the shared secret right now. It does not prove which website you are typing it into: anyone who sees the code within its 30-second window can use it once. Lesson 12 exploits exactly that gap.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tracking sources and checking every citation
md: A citation that exists is not a citation that supports. Checking that every URL resolves catches invented sources but misses the more common failure: a real page cited for a claim it does not make.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Below the API: Inferentia, Trainium, Neuron and SageMaker AI
md: Moving work onto Inferentia or Trainium is a **compiler** project as much as a hardware choice: your model must compile with Neuron, and custom ops may need NKI kernels. Budget engineering time for that, not just instance price.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
md: Speculation is not a correctness risk for your program: wrong-path results never reach registers or memory. It is only a time cost. (It can leak information through caches, which is the Spectre family of attacks; lesson 5 touches on that.)

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: The LSM write path: memtable, flush and immutable SSTables
md: Misconception: "a delete in an LSM-tree frees space immediately." It adds data: a tombstone. Space comes back only when compaction merges the tombstone with every older version of that key and can finally drop both.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: Sequential flooding: how one scan wipes out the hot set
md: Recency alone cannot tell a hot page from a page that was just read once. Every scan-resistant policy adds some second signal: a count, a second reference, or knowledge of which query read the page.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Availability engineering: nines, redundancy and failure domains
md: Nines from a vendor apply to the vendor's component, under its definition of "available". Your service's availability is lower: it multiplies every hard dependency, and redundancy only helps for failures that do not hit all copies at once.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups attackers cannot reach: immutability and isolated recovery
md: Immutable storage is not an immutable backup *system*. If the same admin can change retention for future backups, delete the encryption key, disable the backup jobs or lock everyone out of the console, the attacker wins slowly instead of quickly. Protect the policies, keys and access paths as carefully as the bytes.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Exercising the plan: tabletops, functional tests, failovers and chaos
md: Climb from training to tabletop, functional exercise, full switchover test and continuous chaos experiments. Each needs objectives, success criteria and measured results; the output is a list of gaps with owners, and the measured RTO replaces the guessed one in the plan.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Generating with patches: the BLT decoding loop and its real cost
md: The BLT paper is explicit: its FLOP matching is theoretical, and its implementation may not yet match tokenizer-based models in wall-clock time. Equal FLOPs per byte is a claim about arithmetic, not about latency at batch size 1.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Data races: pthreads in C versus Send and Sync in Rust
md: Implementing Send or Sync by hand is `unsafe impl Send for MyType {}`, one of the five powers in lesson 4. The compiler cannot check it, and the Rustonomicon warns that an incorrect implementation can cause undefined behavior: you are promising that every way to reach the type from two threads is synchronized.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Why one load can cost 3 cycles or 240
md: You never call the cache. The only levers you have are **which addresses you touch and in what order**: data layout and access pattern. That is what the rest of this course makes precise.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Why tracing circuits needs a replacement model
md: Attribution graphs trade the real model for an interpretable stand-in whose direct interactions are linear on one prompt. Every claim read off the graph is a hypothesis about the real model until an intervention confirms it.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels
md: Only clicked documents need propensities, and the estimate is unbiased only if the propensities are correct and every relevant document has a nonzero chance of being observed. Joachims et al. also require that propensities depend only on logged information (unconfoundedness).

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Framework auto-escaping and its escape hatches
md: "It comes from our own API" is not the same as "trusted". The value was typed by some user before your API stored it. React's own Markdown example is safe only because the rendered HTML is shown back to the same user who wrote it, and because the team trusts the Markdown parser to have no bugs.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Temperature: why CLIP multiplies cosines by up to 100
md: The temperature turns a ranking of small cosine gaps into a confident probability. Its value decides how sharply the loss concentrates on hard negatives, which is why CLIP learns it and caps the logit scale at 100 for stability.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Your own rules: key abuse, persistence and log tampering
md: Misconception: "ATT&CK IDs are permanent". MITRE reorganises the matrix: Disable or Modify Cloud Log moved from T1562.008 to T1685.002, and tactics have been renamed. Map rules to IDs, but review the mapping when a new ATT&CK version ships.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Code Spaces 2014: why one account is one blast radius
md: Design as if any one credential will be stolen tomorrow. The test of an architecture is not "can an attacker get in?" but "what can one stolen login destroy or read?" Keep the data and its last good copy behind different identities, in different accounts.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Azure in depth: role assignments, Run Command and PIM
md: In Azure, the keys to escalation are writing role assignments and running code where a privileged identity lives. Make powerful roles eligible through PIM, delegate assignments with conditions instead of Owner, and treat Virtual Machine Contributor on a VM as equal to that VM's managed identity.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Long-lived keys vs temporary credentials: STS and Uber 2016
md: Prefer roles and temporary credentials everywhere. AWS's own best practices say to require human users to use federation with temporary credentials and to require workloads to use IAM roles. Long-term access keys are for the few cases nothing else supports, and they need rotation, monitoring and the narrowest possible permissions.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: What k-means actually optimises
md: Scaling is a modelling choice, not a cleanup step. Standardising says "one standard deviation of every feature counts the same", which silently gives a noisy, unimportant feature as much say as a crucial one. Decide how much each feature should weigh, then scale to match. k-means, DBSCAN's eps and every method in this course measure distance, and none of them is scale free.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels
md: Look at the first two bars. The k = 2 clustering with the *better* inertia, 28.8333, scores ARI 0.4109, while the local optimum with the worse inertia, 30.4167, scores 0.7734. Optimising the objective harder moved the answer away from the truth. Inertia is a proxy, and this is what it means for a proxy to be imperfect: never argue from inertia to correctness.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits
md: Columnar storage cuts bytes moved; vectorized execution cuts instructions per byte. SIMD multiplies the second only when data is dense and in cache.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Why code breaks at -O2: undefined behavior as an optimization license
md: The optimizer assumes the program has no UB: signed overflow never happens, differently typed pointers never alias, dereferenced pointers are not null. Code that breaks those rules can change behavior at -O2. Find it with sanitizers and the -fwrapv, -fno-strict-aliasing and -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks switches, then fix the code.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: A computer-use agent is an ordinary agent loop where the tool is "the computer" and the observation is a screenshot. The model proposes actions in screenshot pixel coordinates; the harness executes them, and is the only place you can enforce scaling, safety and verification.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: loom only sees what goes through loom types. A `std::sync::Mutex` or a third-party lock inside your code still runs, but loom cannot schedule around it, so executions that are possible in reality are silently not modeled. Libraries you depend on need loom support too for full coverage.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
md: Consistency models learn the end of the ODE trajectory, not its slope. The boundary condition anchors the chain at the data; adjacent-time agreement (from a teacher's ODE step or from the data itself) propagates it to high noise; extra steps re-noise and jump again to trade compute for quality.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: The hash ring: each key goes to the next node clockwise
md: Consistent hashing minimises *movement*. It does not by itself give *balance*. With one random token per node, arcs vary wildly in size, as the toy ring shows. The next lesson fixes that.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Why scheduling explodes, and what a constraint model is
md: A constraint solver separates **what** a solution is (the model) from **how** to find it (the search). You declare variables, domains and constraints; the solver chooses the order of guesses and the deductions. Adding a rule means adding one constraint, not rewriting a search loop.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
md: A container is a fenced process on a shared kernel. Threat-model it as "attacker has a shell in this process" and ask which credentials, network paths and kernel interfaces that shell can touch.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: The API server is the front door: authn, authz, admission
md: Every request passes authentication (401 if unknown), authorization (403 if not allowed), then admission (mutate, then validate) before etcd. Reads skip admission, so RBAC alone protects them. Turn on audit logging, because it is off unless you configure it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
md: Pods are non-isolated until a policy selects them. Start each namespace with default deny for both directions, add DNS, then add one allow per intended connection, on both sides.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
md: No single control holds. Minimal signed images, Restricted pods, least-privilege RBAC, default-deny networks, encrypted and narrowly readable Secrets, authenticated node APIs, patched runtimes, and two kinds of detection: each covers what the others miss.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: Do not ask the LLM to copy job ids out of text. Give it the shown list with positions and attributes and let it output a position or an attribute match; code does the lookup. A model that types ids can produce a well-formed id that was never shown.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Do reasoning models admit the hints they use?
md: When the model can act on information without reasoning about it, its CoT usually stays silent about it, even with no pressure to hide. CoT monitoring then helps you notice frequent behaviors, but it cannot certify that a behavior is absent.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
md: A cross-encoder is not a better embedding model. It has no vector output you could store in a vector database. If someone asks you to index a corpus with a reranker, the answer is that you cannot: the score exists only for a specific query.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
md: Ask of every design: which of confidentiality, integrity and authenticity do I need, against whom, and where does the key live? A primitive that gives one goal never silently gives the others.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
md: A random-looking output says nothing about its entropy. Debian's weak keys passed every visual check; their weakness was only visible by counting how many could exist.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Fixed IVs in homemade protocols: Zerologon
md: An IV or nonce is an input with a contract (unique, sometimes unpredictable), not a constant. When a design fixes it, ask what the mode's security proof assumes, who controls the plaintext, and how many attempts an attacker gets. Better: use a standard authenticated protocol instead of designing one.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
md: Every level of the hierarchy does the same thing: stage a tile in a faster, smaller memory and reuse it across as many math operations as the capacity of that memory allows. Tile shapes are the main tuning knobs of a CUTLASS GEMM.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
md: Fast CUTLASS kernels come from a few choices: tile shape (reuse versus occupancy and wave fit), stage count (latency hiding versus shared memory), kernel schedule (cooperative or ping-pong) and the epilogue fusion. CuTe layouts make each choice a type parameter instead of a rewrite.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
md: CXL makes memory placement a policy problem again. The hardware gives you a slower, bigger NUMA tier; the operating system (tiering) or the cluster manager (pooling) must keep hot data local and push only cold or untouched data to it.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
md: Under section 1 a failed attempt can be enough: the offence is about intent and knowledge, not success. 'I didn't get in' is not a defence to trying.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
md: "It's only code" is not an export defence. Sending exploit technology abroad can need a licence, and US rules also cover releasing controlled technology to foreign persons at home (a "deemed export", which the 2021 rule names). Disclosure to the people who will fix the bug is the carved-out case; selling capability is not.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
md: "Nobody asked me directly" is weak protection. Misprision is about *active concealment* of a known felony, and obstruction can be committed by causing others not to disclose. Changing records, drafting the NDA and signing statements you know mislead are acts, not silence.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Upweighting means repeating: epochs, data limits and domain weights
md: Epochs = weight x budget / unique tokens. Up to about 4 epochs repetition costs almost nothing; beyond that each pass is worth less, and by about 40 it is worthless. Cap epochs per domain and give the surplus to domains that still have unique data.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
md: Memory moves in cache lines. Lay out data so that the bytes a hot loop needs are packed together, and the bytes it skips live somewhere else.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Classification: levels, impact and the high-water mark
md: Classify by the damage of disclosure (and of tampering or loss), not by how the data looks. Rate each information type, take the high-water mark for systems, and attach the result as a label that tools can read.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: How DLP recognises sensitive content
md: DLP is only as good as its detector's precision. Prefer labels and exact data match over generic patterns where you can; require context for high confidence; and measure precision on real traffic before turning on blocking. Hashed SSNs are not anonymous: with about a billion possible values, anyone holding the salt can hash them all, so guard the EDM hash file and salt as Restricted data.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
md: Determinism is not one property. Pin the reduction order and you get run-to-run equality. Pin it independently of batch size and position and you get the property a server actually needs. Keep RNG state per request and you get reproducible sampling. Test each one with its own experiment, compare at the logit level, and either go bitwise or attach a measurement to your tolerance.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Least-privilege pipeline credentials: tokens, environments, secrets
md: GitHub's environment docs note that workflows on self-hosted runners are not run in an isolated container, even if they use environments. An environment controls when a secret is released, not what else on that machine can read it afterwards. Pair environments with clean runners (lesson 3).

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Training: a weighted average of masked-LM losses
md: Perplexities reported for diffusion LMs are usually upper bounds (written as a less-or-equal sign in the papers), not exact values. Comparing a bound to an autoregressive model's exact perplexity slightly favours the autoregressive model.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
md: Misconception: "interference only matters at high load." In the timeline there was just one new prompt. Any long prompt that lands in a decode iteration creates a stall for every request in the batch. Load makes it more frequent, not possible.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: What storage remembers: the BTK floppy disk (2005)
md: Deleting a file usually removes the *pointer* to the data, not the data. Recovery works until the space is reused. Everything in the first half of this course is a variation on that sentence.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Live acquisition and encryption: the Ross Ulbricht laptop (2013)
md: Encryption turns *keep it running* into the first forensic step. If you arrive at a decrypted, unlocked machine, you may never get that state back.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO swaps variables: instead of learning a reward and then the policy it implies, it learns the policy directly (the trainable $\pi_\theta$, with weights $\theta$) and reads the reward off it as $\hat r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$. This is the paper's subtitle: your language model is secretly a reward model.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Offline or on-policy: online DPO, and when RL still wins
md: DPO is a strong, cheap offline baseline, not a strict upgrade over RL. Its blind spot is everything the policy generates that the pairs never covered. Fresh on-policy pairs, whether per round (iterative) or per step (online), close much of the gap; tuned on-policy RL still wins in some settings.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
md: Common failure modes: a write path nobody knew about keeps writing only the old store (find it with loud errors and comparisons); deletes resurrected by the backfill; reads switched before the completeness job is rerun; and deleting old data before every reader of the old field is gone.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: The three budgets a model must fit on a small device
md: A model fits a device only if three numbers fit: bytes of weights versus flash, peak bytes of live activations versus RAM, and cycles per inference versus the latency target. Check all three before training anything.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Citrix Bleed, 2023: a length bug that leaked logged-in sessions
md: MFA protects the login, not the session. Anything that leaks or steals a session token after login bypasses MFA completely, which is why session lifetime, session binding and killing sessions after an incident matter.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: End of support, hardening and the replace decision
md: A device that can no longer be patched, or that you cannot trust after a compromise, is not a vulnerability to manage: it is a replacement to schedule. Track support dates like expiry dates and replace before them.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
md: Inference-time levers are cheap but blunt: forcing a stop interrupts reasoning, forcing 'Wait' saturates. Training-time methods (preference pairs, length rewards, LCPO) teach the model to plan a shorter trace, which is why L1 beats budget forcing at small budgets.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control II: App Control for Business, drivers and LOLBins
md: Allowlisting answers "should this code run at all?", a question EDR never asks. Start in audit, read every 3076, block LOLBins you do not need, keep the driver blocklist on, and then treat every 3077 as a signal.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Running edge detection and ON/OFF matching on the toy house
md: Event-based NILM reads each step as one appliance switching. When two appliances switch inside one sample, the switch continuity assumption breaks: the net step looks like a third, unrelated appliance, and the ON/OFF bookkeeping fails for both. Higher sample rates make such coincidences rarer but never impossible.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
md: Each field adds $\log_2(m/u)$. Agreement on a rare value (a domain) is worth far more than agreement on a common one (a city), and a missing field adds nothing instead of counting as a disagreement.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
md: Misconception: deleting a malicious app from Enterprise applications removes it for good. Deleting the service principal removes this tenant's instance; the application object lives in the attacker's tenant, and any user who consents again recreates the service principal. Disable it so it cannot obtain tokens or be consented to.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
md: Misconception: phishing-resistant MFA stops device code phishing. The victim authenticates on the genuine Entra page, so FIDO2 or passkeys work exactly as designed and the tokens still go to whoever started the flow. The fix is to block the flow, not to strengthen the login.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
md: Misconception: the Entra Connect server is 'just a sync box' that a server team can patch and manage like any other. Its connector account can replicate every password hash from AD and its cloud account can write users to the tenant. Microsoft requires treating it as Tier 0.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
md: Readiness is a hint, not a promise. The [select(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/select.2.html) page warns that a socket can be reported readable and a following read can still block, for example when the arrived packet had a bad checksum and was dropped. That is why event loops always use nonblocking sockets.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set
md: Hold out queries, not pairs, and cluster near-duplicates before splitting. Tune on dev as much as you like, read the sealed test set rarely and for decisions you declared in advance, and replace it on a schedule.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Non-executable memory: the NX bit, DEP and W^X
md: NX turns "write code, then run it" into "write data, then crash". It does not stop the hijack of the return address; it removes the attacker's easiest thing to jump *to*.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Why a write steals the whole line: MESI and ownership
md: False sharing needs three things at once: two or more cores, one cache line, and at least one writer. Remove any one (single thread, separate lines, or read-only data) and the line stops bouncing.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Stragglers, partial participation and the round quorum
md: A federated round is a **rendezvous with a quorum**, not a barrier over all clients. The server waits for a minimum percentage of a goal count within a time window, aggregates whoever made it, ignores the stragglers, and abandons the round if too few arrive.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Load imbalance, routing collapse and the auxiliary loss
md: A balance loss is not a free **regularizer** (an extra loss term that nudges the model toward some property). Its gradient changes the router toward balance, not toward predicting the next token. The loss-free paper calls these **interference gradients**, and they are the reason a strong $\alpha$ costs model quality.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Why LLM serving needs its own attention engine
md: Attention in serving is mostly about **memory traffic under irregular shapes**. FlashInfer's answer is to separate what is static (variant, layout, tile sizes: compile time) from what is dynamic (lengths, page lists: a cheap per-step plan).

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Why tests miss bugs that hide in rare interleavings
md: Testing samples behaviors; verification covers all of them. Model checking covers every behavior of a bounded model of the design. Proof covers every behavior of the code, but only for the properties you wrote down.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus on real data: views, quantifiers, triggers and failed proofs
md: A failing assert does not mean the fact is false. With quantifiers it often means no trigger fired. Before weakening the spec, check whether the needed term ever appears in the proof.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
md: Do not copy FP16's overflow handling. FP16 automatic mixed precision (PyTorch's autocast with a dynamic loss scaler) skips the update and shrinks the loss scale when an overflow appears. The FP8 paper explains that overflows are much more likely in FP8's narrow range, so skipping would discard too many steps; FP8 recipes **saturate** out-of-range values to the maximum instead.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Durable means: the bytes reached stable media **and** everything needed to find them (file size, block map, directory entry) did too. `write()` gives you neither; `fsync()` on the file and its directory gives you both.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing good harnesses: fast, deterministic and structure-aware
md: A harness that crashes on its own (a null pointer it should have checked, an `abort()` on documented bad input) floods you with false reports. Treat harness bugs as bugs: the fuzzer is only as trustworthy as the target function.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Symbolic and concolic execution: solving for the input
md: Symbolic execution is not magic search. It struggles with floating point, cryptographic hashes (a solver cannot invert SHA-256), huge loops and code it cannot see, such as system calls. Use it on the narrow, hard checks a fuzzer cannot pass, not as a replacement for fuzzing.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Transpositions and Indel: which edits count changes the answer
md: Two libraries that both say "Damerau-Levenshtein" can disagree, and "ratio" in RapidFuzz is Indel based, not Levenshtein based. When a threshold copied from one tool behaves oddly in another, check which distance and which normalization each uses.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Quad code = coordinates of C and D in the frame where A is (0,0) and B is (1,1). Four numbers, independent of where the quad is, how it is turned, or how big it looks.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
md: H3 parent containment is only approximate. Seven hexagons cannot exactly tile a larger hexagon, so a child cell's area can stick out of its parent's boundary. The index hierarchy is exact logically (truncating an ID always gives the same parent), so aggregating by parent ID is consistent, but do not treat a parent's polygon as the exact union of its children.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Rounding, the small and large pools, and segment sizes
md: Every request is rounded to 512 bytes, routed by size (at most 1 MiB small, otherwise large), and served from a block in that pool. Only a miss touches the driver, with a 2 MiB, 20 MiB or rounded-to-2-MiB segment.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: Speed and capacity trade off at every level: registers and shared memory are on the SM and fast but small, L2 is shared by all SMs, and HBM is large but far away. Kernel design is mostly about making each byte fetched from HBM count.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes
md: The GPU utilization that Nsight Systems reports is **time** utilization, not resource utilization. Its own guide says so: a single running memcpy counts as the same amount of utilization as a huge kernel that takes over all the cores, and concurrent operations in the same chunk can add up to more than 100 percent. A 100 percent busy GPU can still be doing almost nothing useful.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: One kernel, many threads: grids, blocks and SMs
md: Blocks must not depend on each other. A thread may not wait for, or read results produced by, a thread in a different block of the same grid, because that block may not have been scheduled yet. (Thread block clusters, in lesson 4, are the one opt-in exception.)

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Finding communities: modularity and the Leiden algorithm
md: Communities come from edge structure alone. Leiden never reads a description; it only sees nodes and weighted edges. That is why the extraction quality from lesson 2 decides the quality of the topics.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: RLVR changes where the reward comes from, not the RL algorithm. Tulu 3 ran RLVR with PPO; DeepSeek ran it with GRPO. The rest of this course is about GRPO, the algorithm that made RLVR cheap at scale.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Service days, calendar exceptions and times past 24:00
md: A trip runs on date D if its service_id is active on service day D. Its times are offsets from noon minus 12 hours on D, may exceed 24:00:00, and are in agency_timezone. Anything you compute from the schedule must keep the pair (trip_id, service date), not just trip_id.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Reading the numbers: generic events, pitfalls and top-down
md: A sound counter workflow: `perf stat` for IPC and TopdownL1, drill into the biggest bucket with grouped metrics, then `perf record` on the matching event with `:pp` to find the code, change it, and measure again.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
md: These are load counts, not latencies. CPUs keep paging-structure caches and multiple TLB levels with model-specific sizes, so a real miss usually skips some loads. The ratios show the direction of the effect; only a measurement on your hardware gives the size.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
md: The hybrid bet: SSM or linear-attention layers do most of the sequence mixing cheaply, and a handful of full attention layers act as an exact lookup into the past. The Mamba-2 authors put it as SSM layers being a general sequence-to-sequence map while attention layers are "a retrieval mechanism to quickly refer to previous tokens".

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Why BM25 and dense retrieval miss different documents
md: BM25 and dense retrieval fail on different documents. BM25 misses paraphrases; dense retrieval blurs exact identifiers, codes and rare names. Fusing the lists recovers documents either one would miss and promotes documents both agree on.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
md: IT protects data; OT protects people, equipment and the process. The order of priorities is different (safety and availability first), and every defence in this course is shaped by that.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Stuxnet, the controller that lied
md: Stuxnet attacked at the two places defenders trusted most: the engineering software (so the program looked unchanged) and the operator's view (so the process looked normal). The defence is verification through a path the attacker does not control.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
md: Federation replaces many passwords with one trust decision per app: accept whatever this IdP's key signs, after checking it was meant for me, now. Every attack in this course breaks one of those three parts: the key, the checks, or the moment.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Setting up trust: metadata, signing certificates and key rollover
md: Treat the IdP's signing keys and the configuration that says which IdPs and keys are trusted as tier 0 (Microsoft's name for the assets that control every identity in an organisation): the same protection as domain controllers (the servers that hold Active Directory's accounts and keys). Anyone who can change either can become any user without touching a password.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
md: Identity governance answers: should this access exist, who decided, and can we prove it? Every entitlement should trace to a rule or an approved request, and the authoritative record (usually HR) drives the rest.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Privileged access workstations and the clean source rule
md: Session security cannot exceed device security. PAM, bastions and JIT protect the path; the PAW protects its start. Decide at a policy engine using identity, device and approval together, issue short-lived credentials, and enforce at one point.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu turns threshold selection into a 1D search over the histogram: maximize $\omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0-\mu_1)^2$. It works well when changed and unchanged pixels form two separated groups, and only then.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Containment: isolate, watch, disable, block, and the trade-offs
md: Isolating a host is not the same as stopping damage on it. NIST's example: a process that pings a remote host and, when the ping fails after disconnection, encrypts the disk. Capture what you need first when you can.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Ransomware response: pay or not, law enforcement and sanctions
md: Do not read the casino pair as "paying works". As one threat analyst quoted by The Register put it, the incidents are not necessarily comparable: we do not know their scope or which systems and backups were hit. And paying did not stop Caesars' data theft or its notification duties.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Parameterised queries: code and data on separate channels
md: Parameterise every value. Map every identifier and keyword through a fixed allowlist. Never quote a placeholder: in SQLite, `'?'` inside quotes is just a one-character string, and the call fails with "Incorrect number of bindings supplied"; Django's documentation warns against the same mistake with `'%s'`.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: SQPOLL is not a free "go faster" switch. The poll thread consumes a CPU while it spins. io_uring_sqpoll(7) warns it can hurt low-IOPS (few I/O operations per second), bursty or CPU-bound workloads and that it only speeds up submission, not completion handling. Benchmark with and without it.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Fixing ReDoS: rewrite, bound, change engines, cap the input
md: Both V8 modes are experimental, and the blog says the fallback skips patterns with backreferences, lookarounds, large bounded repeats, or the `u` and `i` flags. Treat the flag as a safety net that you test with your own patterns, not as the fix. Rewriting and bounding input are the fixes.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: One skeleton, three allocators: size classes and caches
md: Every production allocator is the same four layers: size classes, a lock-free local cache, a shared per-size-class middle, and a page-level back-end that talks to the OS. The interesting differences are *who owns the local cache* (thread, CPU, or page), *how objects freed by another thread get home*, and *when idle pages go back to the OS*.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
md: Elle never solves for a transaction order. It designs the workload so reads expose the version order, then turns the history into a dependency graph and looks for cycles. A cycle is a concrete, explainable counterexample, and its edge types name the anomaly.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
md: Kernel bypass means the **device driver lives in your process**. Data moves between device and application memory by DMA, the application learns about it by polling memory, and nothing on the per-packet or per-I/O path enters the kernel.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound
md: Misconception: "the GPU is slow at GELU because tanh is expensive". Profile first. A standalone GELU kernel on a large tensor is limited by the read and the write of the tensor, not by tanh.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: A patient and consistent teacher: the recipe that makes KD work
md: Caching teacher outputs is only safe when the student's input is exactly the cached input. With random crops, flips, noise or mixup on the student side, cache the augmentation too or run the teacher live on the same batch. For language models the input is the token sequence itself, so the same rule says: teacher and student must score the same tokens.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: Distillation trades extra training compute (running a teacher) for a cheaper model to serve. It works best when the student can realistically imitate the teacher; when the gap is large, shrink it with an assistant or an easier teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: FP8 without calibration uses a scale of 1.0. That works when values fit FP8's range, but calibrated scales are what vLLM recommends for best accuracy, and some layers (such as sliding-window ones, which attend only to a fixed number of recent tokens) can be kept in the native dtype, the model's own number format.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Hiding the transfer: layer-wise loading and asynchronous saving
md: Overlap turns load plus compute into roughly max(load, compute). It is free speed when the two are balanced and nearly useless when one dominates.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Vector clocks: detecting concurrency exactly
md: Lamport clocks give one-way causality in one integer. Vector clocks give exact causality and detect concurrency, at the cost of one integer per node in every timestamp and every message.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
md: Late interaction is not free accuracy. You pay in index size, in memory bandwidth at query time, and in engine support. For large text corpora a common design is a cheap first stage (BM25 or a single-vector index) with ColBERT or ColPali scoring a few hundred candidates.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: A continuous thought can encode a weighted set of next steps. Deferring commitment is what let Coconut reach 97.0% on ProsQA where CoT reached 77.5%, while generating 14.2 tokens instead of 49.4.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
md: Bounded search costs the leaf's worst-case error on every lookup. Exponential search costs the error of this lookup. Tight models favour bounded search; loose models with mostly good predictions favour exponential search.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Pointwise, pairwise and listwise approaches
md: A common mix-up: these families describe the **training loss**, not the model. A listwise-trained model still scores each document independently at serving time, so serving cost is the same for all three.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
md: Bigger is not a free fix. Raising $d_k$ raises capacity, but state size and per-token compute grow as $d_k d_v$. The research direction instead is a smarter write rule, which is the next lesson.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Users, groups and root: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
md: Setting a user's shell to `/usr/sbin/nologin` or putting `*` in their password field does not fully disable them. The passwd manual notes such users may still run jobs through cron or log in by other means, and an SSH key in their home directory still works if the shell allows it. To retire an account, lock it, expire it and remove its keys.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: SSH: keys versus passwords, authorized_keys and hardening
md: Keys beat passwords because nothing guessable or reusable travels to the server. That moves the risk to the key files themselves: `authorized_keys` decides who gets in, so audit it like you audit sudoers.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: CIS Benchmarks: what one recommendation contains
md: CIS Benchmarks are consensus-written, product-specific configuration baselines with Level 1, Level 2 and STIG profiles. Each recommendation has a rationale, an audit check and a remediation, and maps to other frameworks, so one automated check can serve several auditors.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Writing audit rules that answer real questions
md: Write rules for questions, give every rule a key, use auid>=1000 together with auid!=unset, write b32 and b64 rules on x86-64, put never rules first, keep syscall rules few, and end production rule sets with -e 2.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Linux EDR and fleet telemetry: what sensors see and miss
md: Every sensor has a layer it watches and layers it cannot. Syscall hooks miss io_uring; host tools miss userland rootkits; nothing on the host reliably reports its own removal. Combine kernel-side sensors at LSM or kprobe level with off-host silence alerts.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a fleet plan, and where to practise
md: Inventory, patch, baseline, sandbox, watch, rebuild. Each is ordinary engineering on its own; run together as a loop on every host, they turn a fleet from 2,000 separate risks into one system you can measure.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes
md: A safe default for generation judging: pairwise or rubric grading with the explanation before the verdict; both orders, with disagreement treated as a tie; report and control length; a judge outside the model families being compared; and a human-labelled subset to measure agreement before every major change.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
md: Continuous batching does **not** mean padding requests to a common length. The tokens are packed with no padding, and only attention looks at per-request boundaries. TensorRT-LLM's in-flight batching explicitly requires packed (unpadded) inputs for this reason.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: How vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM put it together
md: Strip away names and every engine is the same loop: a scheduler spending a per-step token budget, a block allocator answering whether it fits, and a policy for when it does not. The engines differ mainly in that last policy and in how they reuse cached blocks.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Designing the filter schema: enums, ranges and nulls
md: A required, non-nullable field such as `salary_max: integer` forces the model to produce a number even when the user said nothing about salary. Constrained decoding guarantees *some* integer, so you get an invented bound (for example 0, or a number copied from a few-shot example) and a filter that silently removes good results.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Latency: the dependency chain decides, not the call count
md: Parallelism is a latency lever, not a cost lever. Running 100 pointwise calls at once reads the same 22,000 tokens as running them one by one, and on a hosted API it uses up rate limits faster.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pairwise ranking prompting: allpairs, sorting and sliding
md: Pairwise preferences are not guaranteed to be transitive: the model can prefer A over B, B over C and C over A. Allpair just counts wins and copes; sorting algorithms assume a consistent comparator, so their output can depend on which pairs they happened to ask. The PRP paper reports robust results anyway but flags this as an open issue.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
md: Float descriptors (SIFT) are compared with L2 distance; binary descriptors (ORB) with Hamming distance. Binary descriptors trade some distinctiveness for much cheaper extraction, storage and comparison.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
md: Garbage collection does not make ABA go away in general. Michael points out that if a program moves the same node back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a stale CAS can still succeed even with perfect GC. What GC (and the schemes in lesson 6) do prevent is the special case where ABA comes from *freeing and reusing* a node someone still references.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
md: Vocabulary trap. "Parsing accuracy" in the 2019 benchmark means grouping, not token-level correctness. Modern papers reserve **PA**, short for parsing accuracy, for the stricter message-level metric where every static token *and* every parameter must be identified correctly, and use **GA** for grouping. A number quoted without its metric is worthless, so always ask: grouping or tokens, per message or per template?

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The pipeline: collect, ship, parse, enrich, store
md: Monitor the pipeline like a production service: events per source per hour, parse-failure rate, queue depth, and the age of the newest event. A sensor that stops sending looks exactly like a quiet, safe network. Also alert on deliberate blinding: Windows event 1102 (Security log cleared) and CloudTrail StopLogging or DeleteTrail calls are ATT&CK Defense Impairment techniques (T1685.005, T1685.002).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Threat hunting and the Pyramid of Pain: the FireEye alert
md: Use indicators (hashes, IPs, domains) for fast, cheap blocking and for searching history after a report is published. Invest your engineering time in behaviour detections, because they are the ones that still work next month.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
md: Online softmax makes attention over KV blocks order-independent. Ring Attention exploits that: queries stay put, KV blocks travel around the ring, and each host needs memory proportional to its block, not to the full sequence.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
md: Convergence is not automatic. The toy update halves the distance to its fixed point each step (it is **contractive**); a learned block carries no such guarantee. Some loops diverge, and Huginn's analysis (lesson 7) finds tokens whose states orbit or drift instead of settling.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
md: Fine-tuning a pretrained model seems to move it along very few useful directions. LoRA turns that observation into an engineering bet: the *change* to each weight matrix during adaptation has low rank (the rank of a matrix is how many independent directions its outputs can point in), so it can be trained and stored as a small factorized update.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: Exact unlearning means the result is what retraining without the forget set would give. SISA keeps that guarantee by confining each point's influence to one shard and one suffix of slices, so only that part is retrained.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
md: NIST notes that most samples blend several categories, so the classic labels are 'considerably less useful than they used to be' for incident handling. Use the labels to communicate quickly; spend your time on behaviour and detection.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Behaviours as indicators: persistence, credentials, ransomware
md: Every behaviour rule has false positives: per-user installers for chat and sync clients legitimately write Run keys from AppData. Sigma's falsepositives field is not decoration; tune with an allowlist of known-good signed programs and review what fires.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Truncation does not make the encoder cheaper. Sentence Transformers' docs stress that a Matryoshka model is not faster or smaller to run. What gets cheaper is everything after encoding: storing, indexing and comparing the vectors.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: SP adds no communication volume: a ring all-reduce is literally a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, so TP + SP moves the same bytes as TP. It just stops storing replicated activations. Per layer memory becomes sbh(34 + 5as/h) / t: everything divided by t.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Finding processes: walking the list versus scanning for tags
md: Scanning finds what the list misses, and also things that are no longer true: exited processes and stale copies of live ones. A psscan-only entry with an exit time is history; one without an exit time whose PID is not in the list is the interesting case.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Case: Ivanti Connect Secure, and a memory-first workflow
md: Memory is where code without files, decrypted configs, live connections and the attacker's last commands live, and it is the first evidence to disappear. Capture it early, verify it, and trust only what two independent views agree on.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Why two threads can disagree about what happened first
md: Reordering is invisible to the thread that does it and visible to every other thread. Memory orderings are a portable contract about which reorderings other threads are allowed to observe.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading
md: Hazard pointers: publish the address, fence, re-validate, then dereference. Retire into a private list and scan when it reaches R. Garbage is bounded by N x R even if threads stall.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: What memory safety means and why breaking it is dangerous
md: A common misconception: "if it didn't crash, it worked". An out-of-bounds write that lands in another variable usually does not crash at all. The program keeps running with corrupted data, which is often worse than crashing.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Why memory-safe languages remove whole bug classes
md: Memory-safe languages do not make programs bug-free, but they turn the bug classes of this course from silent corruption into compile errors or clean crashes. About two thirds of severe bugs in big C and C++ codebases are memory bugs, so moving new code to memory-safe languages removes most of the worst bugs at the source.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
md: Report mAP alongside rank-1, follow the cross-camera protocol, and compare methods only with the same tricks and the same re-ranking setting, because tricks alone can move rank-1 by about 7 points.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
md: Nearly every Miles feature in this course attacks one of two failure modes: GPUs waiting on each other (throughput), or the trainer computing gradients for something other than what was sampled (fidelity).

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Read the case study's reward numbers the way the report does: the nine-step moving average rose from 0.438 to 0.556 over 100 steps, but one run on one task set cannot separate that from run-to-run variation, so it is an observation, not a measured improvement.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The attacker holds the phone: OWASP MAS and its threat model
md: Misconception: "no root detection" is automatically a finding. MASVS states that the absence of resilience measures "does not in itself constitute a vulnerability". It matters only when the profile includes MAS-R, for example to protect against fraud or cheating.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Local authentication: a fingerprint must unlock a key, not a boolean
md: Misconception: "we use Face ID, so the data is protected by Face ID." Only if the data is encrypted under a key that requires it. If the token sits in UserDefaults or SharedPreferences, the prompt protects nothing from someone with the device's files (lesson 4) or a hook (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Build an MLA layer and prove the two forms agree
md: Checklist when porting MLA: normalize the latent only, and cache the normalized latent; rotate only $q^R$ and $k^R$, with the same pair layout as the checkpoint (interleaved here); scale scores by $1/\sqrt{d_h + d_h^R}$, times the YaRN factor for long-context checkpoints; and compare against the plain form before trusting any speedup.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel
md: SGMV groups rows by adapter and runs all segments in one launch, so a batch can mix adapters while the base matmul stays shared. Its cost grows with the number of distinct adapters and their rank, because each one's weights must be read.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Use multi-query when recall is the bottleneck because users word things differently from the corpus, and the next stage can absorb more candidates. Skip it for precise lookups, compound questions (decompose instead), tight latency budgets, and pipelines where a fixed reranker budget already decides the outcome. Measure end-to-end, not just first-stage recall.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
md: These are intuitions, not proofs. The paper itself titles this section 'Why does it work? Some speculation'. Treat them as reasons MTP could help, then check the experiments.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
md: Muon does not produce an exactly orthogonal matrix. The reference implementation's docstring says the result is closer to $US'V^\top$ with the entries of $S'$ roughly uniform in $[0.5, 1.5]$, and that this does not hurt model performance. The Moonlight team also found 10 steps gave a more accurate result than 5 but no better training.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why the best learning rate drifts as models get wider
md: muTransfer has three steps: parametrize the target in muP, tune a smaller version of it, copy the tuned HPs to the target. It works because muP makes the optimal HPs converge to fixed values as width grows.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: muTransfer in practice: what transfers and what it saved
md: Don't expect dropout or weight decay tuned on a small proxy to be optimal for a much larger model trained on different amounts of data. The paper also notes that muTransfer may not be enough for fine-tuning on small datasets, where regularization matters most.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: When spinning wastes the CPU, and how much to spin
md: `spin_loop()` is not `yield` (such as Rust's `std::thread::yield_now()`, which asks the operating system scheduler to run another thread for now). It is a hint to the CPU, not to the scheduler: a thread spinning with it still occupies the CPU for its whole time slice.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Snapshots: how each transaction picks its version
md: Visibility is decided at read time by comparing tuple stamps against the reader's snapshot. Changing *when* the snapshot is taken changes what a transaction sees, without touching the data.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The task: pull typed spans out of running text
md: An NER system is three pieces that must agree with each other: a **tag set** that can represent any set of non-overlapping spans, a **model** that scores tag sequences, and a **decoder** that turns tags back into spans. Most NER bugs live in the seams between them, not in the model.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Picking blocks: importance scores come for free
md: Top-n selection itself is not differentiable, but NSA does not need it to be. The scores come from the compression branch, which is trained by the ordinary language modeling loss through its own output, and the selected tokens are trained through the selection branch's attention. No auxiliary loss is required.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
md: Global hashes, PDQ included, do poorly when one image is a **crop** of another; the PDQ document lists deep crops as out of scope. ImageHash's documentation shows how fast aHash degrades with rotation on its test image: 2 bits at 1 degree, 11 at 6 degrees, 21 at 26 degrees. Large borders, overlaid text and memes also defeat them.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: DHCP starvation and rogue DHCP servers
md: Whoever answers DHCP chooses a device's gateway and DNS server, so a rogue DHCP server is an on-path attack on every device it reaches. Only trusted ports may send DHCP server messages.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Segmentation, zero trust and the Target breach
md: Segmentation limits how far one compromise spreads; zero trust removes network location as a reason to trust anything. Both assume a breach will happen, and both only pay off when someone watches the alerts at the boundaries.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: What TLS still reveals, and fingerprinting clients with JA3
md: A fingerprint identifies a TLS library and its configuration, not an intention. Python, Go and Windows programs share fingerprints with malware written in the same language or on the same stack. Use JA3 to cluster and to rank leads, never as a verdict on its own.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: From bits on a wire to packets
md: Every packet is a header plus a payload. Every device on the path must read the header to deliver it, and can read the payload too unless it is encrypted. Both facts drive almost everything in network security.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTPS and TLS at a glance: what encryption hides and what it does not
md: TLS protects the content of one connection between two endpoints. It does not hide who talks to whom, it does not make the server trustworthy, and it does not protect data once it is decrypted at either end.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Policy = mode + nodes + scope, applied at allocation time. Use bind for strict isolation, preferred when spilling over is acceptable, interleave for big shared data, and leave private per-thread data on the default local policy.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: What a detector outputs, and how two boxes are compared
md: A detector outputs a variable-size set of (box, class, score) triples, and IoU between boxes is the measure every later stage builds on.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
md: Pick the counting method by scene: detection when objects are separable and you need locations, density maps for dense crowds where boxes fail, and tracking plus line or region events for video, where the same object appears in many frames.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
