md: Never compute a rate as last value minus first value over a counter. One restart in the window turns a positive rate into a large negative number, and `rate()` exists precisely to handle that case for you.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
md: OCR is a chain: detect, then recognize, then order and extract. Each stage only sees the previous stage's output, so an early error silently becomes a wrong field later.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The kernel/user boundary: rings and the system call door
md: User programs run in ring 3 and can only ask; the kernel runs in ring 0 and decides. A system call is the only door between them. Sandboxing is mostly the art of closing doors and narrowing what each open door accepts.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Sandboxes: Chrome's broker model, macOS and iOS
md: A broker is only as good as its request checking. A broker that performs "open this path" for any path a renderer names has turned itself into a tool for the attacker. That failure has a name, the confused deputy, and it is the subject of lesson 15.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Your own footprint while investigating: OPSEC and bias
md: Investigating leaves traces. Use a separate, logged-out research environment, expect the other side to read its logs, and record your exact queries because results differ by engine, location and history.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Geolocation: finding where a picture was taken
md: List clues, bound the area, eliminate candidates with the most distinctive clue first, then confirm with an independent feature. Report what matched and what could not be checked.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Putting it together: an ethical OSINT review, and where to practise
md: An ethical OSINT engagement is authorised, planned, minimal, preserved, verified and reported with its limits, and it ends with fixes and deleted working data.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: CI is a contract written in the repo: on these events, on these machines, run these commands, and block the merge unless they exit with status 0. Read `.github/workflows/` before your first PR to a project.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Misconception: a reviewer who leaves 15 comments is blocking you on all 15. Often most are optional. If the reviewer did not say which ones block the merge, ask instead of guessing.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: Read in this order before you touch code: LICENSE (can you contribute at all), CONTRIBUTING (how), CODE_OF_CONDUCT (how to behave), SECURITY (if your finding is a vulnerability). Ten minutes of reading avoids a rejected PR.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
md: Rebase rewrites history. The rule from Pro Git, the free Git book on git-scm.com: do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on. Your own PR branch is the usual exception, which is why the next lesson's force-push needs care, not a ban.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
md: Public is not the same as open source. Code you can read on GitHub with no license file is all rights reserved, and so is a snippet whose license you never checked.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: CLA: one signed agreement per person or company, granting rights up front. DCO: no agreement, just a per-commit certification of origin via Signed-off-by, checked mechanically by email match.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Map the repository before you read a line of it
md: A common mistake is to fix a bug inside a generated file. Your edit is overwritten the next time the generator runs, and reviewers will reject it. When a file says *do not edit*, find its input (here `src/commands/get.json`) in the build rule and change that instead.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: Every cut is an experiment: remove, rerun, compare to the original failure. Keep cuts that preserve the exact error; undo the rest.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
md: If the project squash-merges PRs, your intermediate commits disappear from the main branch anyway, and the PR as a whole becomes one commit. That makes **one logical change per PR** even more important: the squash cannot separate a fix from a speedup after the fact.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: Paging is not free. The paper measured 20 to 26% higher attention kernel latency than FasterTransformer's kernel, from block-table lookups, extra branches and variable lengths. It still wins end to end because only the attention operator pays, and the larger batch more than makes up for it.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: When authorisation is unclear: the Iowa courthouse arrests
md: Ambiguity is what got two professionals arrested. Write down: who owns each target, who signed for it, when testing may happen, who outside the client has been told, and two 24/7 ways to reach someone who can confirm it.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Why profilers sample stacks instead of timing every call
md: A sampling profiler answers one question: what fraction of CPU samples had this function on the stack? It is cheap because work happens per sample, not per call, and it is approximate because it is a sample.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
md: Common misconception: "unflushed stores are lost on a crash." Some are, some are not, and the hardware chooses. Treat each dirty cache line as independently maybe-persisted. Flushes give you a lower bound on what is durable, never an upper bound.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Envelope, header and display name: why spoofing works
md: Authentication checks answer "was this domain's use authorised?", never "is this message honest?". A display-name spoof or lookalike domain passes them cleanly. Defences need both: DMARC against exact-domain spoofing, and human-facing cues plus process rules for the rest.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
md: Two rules give every struct layout: **each field's offset is a multiple of its alignment**, and **the struct's size is a multiple of its own alignment** (the largest field alignment). Everything else, including all the padding, follows from these.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
md: A top-down pose model inherits every mistake of its detector. If two people overlap and NMS merges their boxes, or the detector misses someone, the keypoint network has no way to recover that person. The authors of OpenPose, the bottom-up system in lesson 3, call this **early commitment**: the pipeline commits to the detector's boxes before it has looked at a single joint.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Pre-filtering: allow lists and brute force over the matches
md: Pre-filtering with a flat scan is exact and its cost is proportional to the number of matches, $sn$. That makes it the best plan for restrictive filters and the worst plan for broad ones.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Bandwidth-bound code: count the bytes, skip the reads
md: Do not sprinkle streaming stores everywhere. Intel recommends them for memset-style fills larger than about half the last-level cache when the data is not read soon after. On Skylake server it warns that overusing them on smaller blocks evicts lines you need and can hit a per-core limit on non-temporal write bandwidth.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: k-anonymity: generalise and suppress until you hide in a crowd
md: k-anonymity is a property of one table against one declared set of quasi-identifiers. It says nothing about columns you forgot, other releases, or what the sensitive values in a class reveal.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy in real systems: units, trust and hazards
md: "We use differential privacy" is not a guarantee until you know three things: epsilon (and delta), the unit of privacy, and who sees the raw data. A large epsilon at event level with a trusted curator can protect very little.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Private set intersection: comparing lists without sharing them
md: Diffie-Hellman PSI works because blinded exponentiation commutes: H(x)^(ab) = H(x)^(ba). Each side blinds with a secret it never reveals, so only matching items line up. Hashing alone is not PSI, because hashes of small identifier spaces can be inverted.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 1: reading sudo rules like an auditor
md: Misconception: "NOPASSWD is the dangerous part." It does remove a hurdle for an intruder who has a shell but not the password (a web shell, a stolen SSH key). But a rule that leads to a shell is a root grant with or without a password prompt. Fix what the command can do first, then decide on the password.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: How a PRM is trained and how it scores a solution
md: A PRM is a per-step classifier read off in one forward pass. Training labels stop at the first error. To compare solutions you reduce step scores to one number; product and minimum perform similarly, but product quietly favours shorter solutions.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Generative PRMs: verifiers that reason before they judge
md: Generative PRMs phrase verification as text generation: write a step-by-step critique, then read the verdicts and a Yes probability off it. They need far fewer labels and lead on error location, at the price of many more tokens per verification and overconfident scores.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
md: Misconception: "more threads means more parallelism." Parallelism is capped by the number of cores. Past that, extra CPU-bound threads only take turns: they add involuntary switches, push answers later, and make threads evict each other's cache. Extra threads help only when they spend time blocked, as in the I/O scene.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: DSPy: signatures, modules and optimizers
md: Every bootstrap and search optimizer trusts the metric. The DSPy docs warn that a non-deterministic metric (for example an LLM judge) makes the chosen demos "a function of metric noise as much as program quality". Make the metric deterministic where you can, validate any LLM judge against humans first, and keep a held-out set.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Why security teams script, and your first Python program
md: A script is the steps you would do by hand, written down once so they run the same way on every line. Its biggest risk is not crashing; it is quietly counting the wrong thing.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Hashing files and checking them against known-bad lists
md: Hash files in binary chunks, normalize every indicator to lowercase before comparing, and remember that a match means "known bad" while a miss means only "not this exact file".

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym filters in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch
md: Create the synonym set before the index that references it. Elastic's guide warns that an index pointing at a missing set becomes inoperable and must be deleted and re-created, or closed and re-opened.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension
md: Binary quantization = sign of each coordinate, compared with XOR and popcount. It buys 32x memory and very cheap comparisons, but the distance it produces is coarse and has no error guarantee.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Discounts, refunds and rewards: value that can be claimed twice
md: v2 is right for requests that arrive one at a time, and still wrong when two refunds arrive at the same instant: both can read "120 left to refund" before either is recorded, and both pay out 100. Every check of the form "read a total, decide, write" is also a race condition. Lessons 5 to 9 make it atomic.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Fixing races in the database: atomic updates, locks, constraints
md: Put the check inside the write, or lock before you read, or let a constraint say no. Then make the database refuse the bad end state too (CHECK, UNIQUE), so a race you missed fails loudly instead of paying out.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to logic and race abuse
md: Log every value-changing event with business context, alert on impossible patterns (one-time actions that succeed twice, bursts within milliseconds, flows faster than a human), and reconcile balances against ledgers. Then contain before you investigate, and retest fixes in parallel.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Indexing: how chunk size and overlap decide what can be found
md: Small chunks lose their context. D1.5 reads *or adoption. Send leave requests to the People team, who approve them.* It never says which leave. In a real handbook with ten leave policies it would match every leave question equally well. Bigger chunks keep context but dilute the embedding and spend more of the prompt.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Feature logging: train on exactly the numbers you serve
md: Features used for training must be produced by the same code, against the same index state and at the same moment as the features used for serving. Log the vector at query time; do not reconstruct it later.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Trust among thieves: exit scams, takedowns and a fragmented market
md: "The group promised to delete the data" is not evidence. LockBit kept data of victims who paid (found in Operation Cronos), BlackCat cheated its own affiliate, and leaked chats from other groups named victims who had paid for silence. Plan as if stolen data will eventually be published.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: The ransom decision: negotiation, proof of life and sanctions
md: A passed proof-of-life test proves only that the actor can decrypt the files tested. Test every size class you need, especially the largest databases and virtual disks, and price the decryptor against what your surviving backups can already restore.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
md: In practice: register big pools on huge pages, keep the number of connected QPs bounded (share, or use UD for fan-out), batch posts behind one doorbell, inline small payloads, signal selectively, avoid hot atomics, and handle error completions by resetting or recreating the connection.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
md: Treating a blank as a rating of 0 is a modelling choice, not a fact. It makes plain cosine reward items that are merely *rated by the same people*, whatever the ratings. In Sarwar et al.'s MovieLens experiments, adjusted cosine gave lower error (mean absolute error, the average size of the gap between predicted and true rating) than plain cosine or Pearson correlation.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
md: Split by time, exclude what the user already consumed, beat tuned simple baselines, and confirm with an online experiment.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
md: A GROUP BY result from a HashAggregate has no defined order. If you need sorted output, write ORDER BY; do not rely on the order you happened to see.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
md: Misconception: reward hacking means the RL algorithm is buggy. DeepMind's analysis points the other way: the behavior comes from misspecification, and a *better* optimizer is more likely to find an intricate loophole that a weaker one would miss. Stronger RL makes the specification matter more, not less.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Governance, risk and compliance: three jobs and who decides
md: Governance decides who decides. Risk management decides what is worth doing. Compliance proves to outsiders that you did what you are obliged to do. They overlap, but a company can be compliant and still badly governed, or well governed and still breached.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Security economics: how much to spend (the Gordon-Loeb model)
md: Gordon-Loeb's lessons for engineers: spend where a dollar reduces the most expected loss, not where the scariest weakness is; for the paper's broad families of breach functions the optimum is at most about 37 percent of expected loss; and making controls more effective beats making budgets bigger.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: One control, many frameworks: CIS Controls, HIPAA and the crosswalk
md: Do not run one programme per framework. Write each control once, build it to the strictest applicable requirement, map it to every framework it satisfies, and attach evidence that is collected automatically. Start from CIS IG1 if you have nothing; use the crosswalk to answer everyone else.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
md: Insurance does not replace controls or accountability. Regulators still fine you, customers still leave, and a claim can fail if your application overstated your controls or the event falls under an exclusion. Treat the policy wording as a contract engineers should read: what counts as a covered event, which notice deadlines apply, which incident responders you must use.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: After new weights land, cached KV entries are wrong: they were computed by the old weights. SGLang's `update_weights_from_distributed` flushes the cache by default, and AReaL's interruptible workers discard KV caches and recompute them with the new weights before continuing unfinished sequences.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: One fault, 397 alerts: collapsing the storm
md: Dedup and grouping are lossless: they change how many notifications you receive, not what was observed. Inhibition and silences are lossy: they delete evidence from your view. Use the first two freely and the last two sparingly.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: Do not confuse RRF's k with the k of k-nearest-neighbors. Azure AI Search's docs stress that the RRF constant is "entirely separate" from the k that sets how many neighbors a vector query returns. Elasticsearch names them `rank_constant` and `rank_window_size` to avoid the clash.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: From -ENOMEM and ERR_PTR to Result
md: `to_result` is not a general converter. For a C function that returns a byte count or an index on success, use the raw value: check `< 0` yourself or write a small wrapper that returns `Result<usize>`. Otherwise the success value silently disappears.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The baseline you replace: EEVDF picks and the knobs it offers
md: Misconception: a shorter slice buys a task more CPU. Under EEVDF it buys an earlier deadline and more, shorter turns; the total still follows the weights.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Build, load and run your own scheduler end to end
md: Misconception: the loader is just a launcher and can exit once the scheduler is attached. The link belongs to the process: when it exits, the link is destroyed and the kernel unregisters the scheduler. The loader is also the only place the exit reason gets printed.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring and debugging a scheduler
md: Misconception: a lower average latency means a better scheduler. A policy can cut the median and still multiply the p99, and for interactive work the tail is what users feel.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558 and a signing key that should have died in 2021
md: A signing key's real lifetime is not what the plan says but what the system enforces. Enforce expiry in code, alert on key age, and treat "we paused rotation" as a security incident with an owner and a deadline.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: JavaScript: prototype pollution and code built from strings
md: Pollution is process-wide and lasts until restart. One request can change the behaviour of every later request to that Node.js process, including other users' requests, which makes it confusing to debug and dangerous to leave running.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Heartbleed as a diff: reviewing every field of a message
md: Field checklist for any parser diff: list every value taken from outside, and for each one point to the line that validates it against a fact the code controls (the real buffer length, a maximum). An empty cell is a finding. For pointer loops, end checks use < or >=, never == or !=.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Secure channels at every layer: what each protocol protects
md: Ask two questions of any secure protocol: between which two points does the protection start and stop, and what happens to the data outside them? A VPN stops at the gateway; SSH stops at the server process; S/MIME never stops while the message stays encrypted.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Time is a security input: NTP, delay attacks and NTS
md: NTS stops forged and altered time replies; it cannot stop delay attacks, because a delayed packet is still authentic. RFC 8915 bounds the damage at MAXDIST/2 and suggests several time sources or several network paths. Combine NTS with multiple servers and alert on large clock steps.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: The perimeter model, Operation Aurora and the road to BeyondCorp
md: Zero trust does not mean "no VPN" or "no firewall". BeyondCorp removed the trust that came with being on the network. Encrypted tunnels and network filters still exist in zero trust designs; they just stop being the reason anyone gets access.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Measuring the journey: CISA's maturity model and a migration plan
md: A maturity score measures capabilities, not outcomes. An agency can be Advanced in every pillar and still be breached through an unpatched edge appliance. Track both: the stage per pillar, and evidence such as how many apps still need a VPN and how many accounts still use phishable MFA.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Worked scenario: prompt injection through attacker-written log fields
md: Anything an attacker can write into a log can end up in your model's context. Give the model no authority the attacker should not have, let deterministic rules make decisions, and treat instruction-like text in a field as an indicator.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Attack surface, and the Morris worm's four doors
md: Attack surface is everything an attacker can touch: services, features, trust relationships and people. The Morris worm used all four kinds at once. The cheapest defence is removing doors you do not need (a debug command in production, an unused service); the next is making each remaining door check its input.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
md: Real attacks do not walk the phases neatly in order. Attackers loop (discover, move, discover again), skip steps (a stolen password needs no weaponization), and run phases in parallel. Use the models as a vocabulary and a checklist, not a script.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Executive summaries: one page for the person who decides
md: Do not soften the verdict to keep a client happy, and do not dramatise it to be noticed. Both destroy the summary's main asset: that the reader can take it at face value. If the news is good, say so plainly; a calibrated "the defences held" is as useful as a warning.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
md: A common misconception: self-play means no external signal. Games have a perfect, free judge: the rules decide who won. Take that away and a model playing against itself only amplifies its own beliefs, which is the collapse setting from the prerequisite course.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Provider prompt caching is a different thing from semantic caching
md: They stack. Check the semantic cache first; on a miss, send a request whose stable content comes first so the provider's prefix cache can reuse it. Prompt caching is safe to turn on everywhere; a semantic cache needs the threshold and scoping work from the previous lessons.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell: how logging a string ran code
md: Log4Shell is injection in a place nobody thought was an interpreter. Logging user input is normal and correct; the library silently treated part of that input as template syntax with network access. Recall the injection course: whenever data is evaluated, the evaluator is the attack surface.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
md: Chunked prefill trades the long prompt's time to first token for bounded step size: lower peak activation memory (activations are the intermediate tensors a forward pass keeps, and they grow with the number of tokens in the pass) and, when decodes are mixed in, steadier token gaps for everyone else. It does not reduce total prefill work.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: CH trades a one-time preprocessing pass (contract nodes, add shortcuts) for tiny queries: two upward searches that meet at the most important node of the route, then shortcuts are unpacked back into original roads.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: Misconception: "wider vectors always mean proportionally faster code." Width is only the upper bound. Memory bandwidth, latency chains and loop overheads decide how much of it you actually get.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
md: Allocators are not just faster or slower `malloc`s. Each design gives up a freedom (free in any order, any size, any type) and gets speed or lower fragmentation in return. Ask which freedom your workload can give up.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: "Disaggregated" here is about trainer versus rollout GPUs. It is unrelated to PD (prefill-decode) disaggregation (`--prefill-num-servers`), which puts SGLang's prefill (processing the whole prompt in one pass) and decode (generating one token at a time) on different servers, and it does not imply async training by itself.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Verdicts, severity and priority: true, false and benign positives
md: Using a rule's historical precision in priority has a trap: a rule that is usually wrong will sink to the bottom forever, including the one time it is right. Precision should make you fix the rule, not ignore it. Target's "malware.binary" alerts are the cautionary tale.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Pivoting, building a timeline, and mapping it to ATT&CK
md: Do not force-fit. If you cannot say which technique an event shows, write the plain fact and leave the ID out. A wrong mapping in a case note propagates into reports and detection gap analyses.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Voice clones and deepfake meetings: when seeing is not believing
md: Misconception: "train people to spot deepfakes". Spotting artefacts is a losing race as tools improve, and the IC3 itself says AI content is often hard to identify. Teach the artefacts as a reason to pause, but make the decision depend on an independent channel.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Why single neurons are hard to read: superposition
md: Superposition: a layer with $d$ dimensions can represent many more than $d$ sparse features as almost-orthogonal directions, at the cost of interference. Neurons then mix many features, so we look for directions instead.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
md: High variance explained is not full understanding. Sonnet's SAEs explained at least 65% of variance, so a sizeable part of the activation lives in the error term, and a latent's top activating examples do not prove what it does. Use ablation or steering to check.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
md: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in 2D or 3D coordinates. Simple kriging is the zero-mean GP on residuals; ordinary kriging adds an unknown constant mean; universal kriging adds trend basis functions; the nugget is observation noise.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
md: Not every tree method is lossless. Medusa's optional **typical acceptance** keeps a candidate if the target's probability exceeds $\min(\epsilon, \delta e^{-H(p)})$, a threshold that depends on the entropy $H$. It raises speed at higher temperatures but no longer samples from the target's distribution. Medusa-2 also changes the backbone weights, so outputs differ from the original model.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
md: Long-form and streaming ASR are decoding problems layered on a fixed-window model: the window moves by predicted timestamps, unstable text waits for agreement, and silence must be removed or detected before the decoder invents something to say.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Beyond the basic chunk: size classes, thread caches and fragmentation
md: Fast allocators round requests to size classes, serve each class from same-size slabs or spans, and put a lock-free per-thread or per-CPU cache in front. The costs are bounded rounding waste, memory parked in caches, and spans pinned by a few live objects.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: When RAM runs out: page cache, file mappings, swap and thrashing
md: Clean file pages are cheap to evict, dirty ones need write-back, and anonymous ones need swap. The kernel approximates LRU with reference bits and active/inactive lists, but once the working set exceeds RAM, even a 0.1 percent miss rate makes memory 100 times slower: thrashing.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
md: Two different knobs, often confused. The bound $B$ moves the watermark (how long to wait before the first result). The allowed lateness $L$ keeps state after that (how long to accept corrections). Raising $B$ delays every result; raising $L$ costs state memory and extra firings but does not delay the first result.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Scaled dot-product attention, computed on four tokens
md: Attention output for a position = softmax(its query dotted with every key, divided by the square root of d_k), used as weights on the value vectors. Every step is a matrix multiply or a row-wise softmax, so all positions are computed at once.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: One layer end to end, in numbers and in code, and how it decodes
md: One layer: attention adds a cross-position change, add & norm, the FFN adds a per-position change, add & norm. At inference the encoder runs once and the decoder runs once per output token, with beam search choosing among the most probable partial outputs.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25 in Lucene and Elasticsearch: fields, tuning, limits
md: BM25 only matches the terms you typed, after analysis. A document saying "low-cost airfare" scores 0 for cheap flights. Synonyms, stemming, query expansion (adding related terms to the query), or a dense retriever (a neural network maps query and documents to vectors, ranked by vector similarity) are needed for vocabulary mismatch, which is why many systems combine BM25 with vector search.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
md: The training loop is the generic one (forward, cross-entropy, backward, clip, AdamW step), and the GPT-specific knowledge is in the settings: small normal init with scaled residual projections, decoupled weight decay on matrices only, warmup then cosine decay, and big token batches via gradient accumulation.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Integrals: accumulated change and area under a curve
md: An integral adds up infinitely many thin slices $f(x)\,dx$. To evaluate one, find an antiderivative and subtract its values at the ends; when no antiderivative is available, add up trapezoids numerically.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Jacobians: derivatives of vector-valued functions
md: The Jacobian generalizes the derivative to vector outputs, and the chain rule becomes a product of Jacobians. Backprop never forms those matrices: it carries one row (the loss gradient) backward and multiplies it into each layer's Jacobian, giving $W^\top$ products for inputs and outer products for weights.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Writing scripts: arguments, tests, if, loops and functions
md: `if`, `while`, `&&` and `||` all branch on an exit status. `[` and `test` are commands that turn a comparison into a status. Functions return a status with `return` and data on standard output.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Job control and signals: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, background jobs and trap
md: Reaching for `kill -9` first is a habit worth breaking. SIGKILL gives the program no chance to flush buffered output, remove lock or temporary files, or stop its own child processes, which can be left running as orphans. Send SIGTERM, give it a few seconds, then escalate.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
md: Static word embeddings (one fixed vector per word, whatever the sentence) encode co-occurrence statistics. Similar vectors mean *used in similar contexts*, which often but not always means *similar meaning*: antonyms like hot and cold share many contexts too.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
md: Prefill is math-bound (many tokens share each weight read). Decode is memory-bound (one token per weight read). Most GPU time in a long answer goes to decode, and the floor for each decode step is weight bytes divided by bandwidth.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Bits, bytes and hex: how numbers are stored
md: Bits have no type. The byte `0xf4` is 244, or -12, or part of a jump instruction, depending on which instruction reads it. Hex is a compact way to write bits: one digit for every 4 bits.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
md: Simplified model. Real CPUs have several cache levels, and **hardware prefetchers** detect sequential and strided access (every k-th element, a fixed step apart) and fetch lines before they are asked for, hiding much of the cost of row order (and some of column order). Measured slowdowns vary by machine; the direction does not.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From web crawl to training tokens: the pretraining data pipeline
md: More deduplication is not automatically better. FineWeb first deduplicated all 96 snapshots against each other, which left 4T tokens and barely beat no deduplication. In the oldest snapshot, the 10 percent of data that survived was worse than the 90 percent removed (more ads and keyword lists). Deduplicating each snapshot on its own, about 20T tokens, matched the strong RefinedWeb dataset.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Policy gradients: how a score becomes a gradient
md: Policy gradient = average of advantage times the gradient of the log-probability of what was sampled. Baselines and value models cut the noise without biasing it, GAE spreads one final score into per-token advantages, and the ratio rho lets one batch of samples be reused.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
md: The base of the log in idf does not change the ranking: switching from log10 to ln multiplies every idf by the same constant (about 2.303), so every score scales equally. What does matter is the shape, for example whether tf is raw or sublinear.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Multi-file C: headers, include guards, static, extern and make
md: A missing header in a prerequisite list gives silent stale builds. With `main.o: main.c` only, changing SQUARE to a cube in square.h rebuilt area.o alone, and app still printed 9 instead of 27. List every header, or let the compiler do it: `-MMD` makes GCC and Clang write a .d file of each source's user-header dependencies for the Makefile to include.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
md: Every malloc needs exactly one matching free, on every path out of the function. Missing it leaks memory; doing it twice, or touching the block afterwards, is undefined behavior that can corrupt the allocator's own bookkeeping.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
md: 'It runs fine' is not evidence that C code is correct. A clean run without sanitizers says almost nothing about memory safety; even a clean sanitizer run covers only the paths your inputs exercised.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1
md: Assigning, passing, or returning a non-`Copy` value moves it. To keep using the original, either `clone()` it (pay for a copy) or lend it out with a reference (next lesson).

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
md: `clone()` everywhere and `Rc<RefCell<T>>` everywhere make errors go away but give up what ownership buys you: clones cost time and memory, and `RefCell` turns compile-time guarantees into run-time panics. Reach for them when the data really has no single owner, not to silence the checker.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
md: Not every useful function is linear. $f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} \ne 0$ is **affine**: it moves the origin, so $f(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{b}$ instead of $\mathbf{0}$. Neural network layers are affine, and their activation functions (like ReLU, explained next) are not linear at all. That nonlinearity is what lets a deep network do more than one big matrix could.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The SVD: rotate, stretch, rotate, then keep what matters
md: Every matrix is rotate, stretch, rotate: $A = U\Sigma V^\top$. $\sigma_1$ is the spectral norm, $\sigma_1/\sigma_n$ the condition number, the count of nonzero $\sigma_i$ the rank. Truncating to the top $r$ terms is the best rank-$r$ approximation, and PCA is the SVD of centered data.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Many features: linear regression in matrix form and feature scaling
md: Compute $\mu$ and $\sigma$ on the **training** data only and reuse those same numbers for validation, test and production inputs. Computing them on all the data leaks information from the held-out rows into training (lesson 11).

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Bias and variance: where the U-shaped test curve comes from
md: High variance is not the same as high training error. The degree-9 fit has zero training error and the largest variance; its errors show up only on new data.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
md: A hidden layer only adds power because of the nonlinearity between layers. Without it, any stack of layers is one linear map in disguise.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The cost of backprop: compute, activation memory, checkpointing
md: Backprop's compute is a small constant times the forward pass, about two more matrix multiplies per layer. Its memory is the real constraint: every activation from the forward pass stays alive until its layer's backward step, unless you pay compute to recompute it.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: paging, page tables and the TLB
md: The offset is never translated, and the page table is per process. Two processes can use the same virtual address 21 and reach completely different physical bytes; that is the isolation, not a bug.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency bugs: atomicity, ordering and deadlock
md: A deadlock-prone program can run correctly many times, because the deadlock needs an unlucky interleaving. Testing does not show it is safe; a lock order does.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
md: Independent is not the same as mutually exclusive. Mutually exclusive events ("sum is 2" and "sum is 12") cannot both happen, so learning one happened tells you the other did not: they are strongly *dependent*. Independence means the joint probability factorizes, $P(A \cap C) = P(A)P(C)$.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Why averages are stable: the law of large numbers and the CLT
md: Noise in an average shrinks as $1/\sqrt n$. That single scaling law explains why larger batches give smoother gradients, why small evals are noisy, and why A/B tests need large samples to detect small effects.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test
md: Every test in this lesson is the same move: estimate, compute its standard error from the variance rules and the CLT, and ask how many standard errors the estimate sits from the null. Significance depends on sample size as much as on effect size.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Run your own scaling study: sweep, fit, extrapolate, error bars
md: Never report a scaling-law forecast without two checks: refit from several starts with tight tolerances and confirm they agree, and bootstrap the runs to get a range. A single unconverged fit can be off by 2x and still look perfectly reasonable.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Graded relevance and nDCG: rewarding the best result first
md: IDCG must come from **all** judged documents in the qrels, not from re-sorting the documents your run retrieved. Re-sorting only the retrieved ones gives IDCG 5.193 and nDCG@10 = 0.674 instead of 0.576, and hides the fact that the run missed d9 entirely. trec_eval builds the ideal from the qrels.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Training embeddings with in-batch negatives
md: Contrastive training with in-batch negatives is what turns a language model into an embedding model: pull each true pair together, push everything else in the batch apart, with a scale (temperature) that controls how sharply.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Byte-level BPE: how GPT-2 and its successors tokenize anything
md: Byte-level BPE = UTF-8 bytes as the base alphabet (256 symbols, so nothing is ever unknown) + a regex pre-tokenizer that limits where merges can happen + an ordered merge list. Decoding concatenates bytes and is lossless.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
md: He et al. report that their 30-layer plain ReLU network trained with He initialization while the Xavier-initialized version *completely stalled*, with all gradients diminishing. Yet on their 22-layer model both converged (He init just started reducing error earlier), and on a smaller model the final accuracies were about the same. A bad init does not always crash; past some depth it silently stops learning.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Instrumenting a run: gradient norms, update ratios, activation stats
md: Log per step: loss, global gradient norm and learning rate. Log per layer: update-to-weight ratio (about 1e-3), activation std and dead fraction. Each failure in this course has a signature: shrinking scale with depth and ratios near 1e-8 for a bad init; ratios near 1e-2, dead units and a climbing gradient norm for too high a rate.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Dependencies and transitive trees: code you never chose
md: Misconception: "I only use five packages." You use five packages plus everything they pull in. Count with `npm ls --all | wc -l` or `pip list` inside a fresh virtual environment, and you will usually find one to two orders of magnitude more.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: SBOMs: an ingredients list you can query when the alarm rings
md: An SBOM is a claim about contents, only as complete as the tool that wrote it. It lists what is present, not whether any of it is malicious, and an SBOM made from source can miss what the build pulled in. Generate it from the built artifact, sign it, and keep it with the artifact.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
md: The question is not whether synthetic data enter the loop, but whether real data stay in it. Keep the original human data, keep adding fresh real data, and treat synthetic data as an addition. Even then, a fixed share of mismatched synthetic data floors the error, so its quality matters as much as its quantity.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When a system call blocks: sleeping, short counts and EINTR
md: Retrying `EINTR` is right for `read` and `write`. For calls with a timeout (`poll`, `epoll_wait`, `nanosleep`), retrying with the original timeout restarts the clock, so a steady stream of signals could stretch the wait without limit. Recompute the time left before retrying.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Watching and restricting system calls: strace, faults and seccomp
md: Trust strace's counts more than its times. Tracing stops the program at every call, so `-c` and `-T` times are inflated, and calls served by the vDSO never appear at all (the cost lesson). Measure speed without strace, for example with `perf stat`, and use strace to learn what the program does.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Taming the tail: hedged requests and honest reporting
md: Honest tail reporting: record every request into a mergeable histogram (HdrHistogram or bucketed histograms), measure from intended start under a load plan, merge histograms rather than percentiles across machines, and report several high percentiles plus the max, with the sample count.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
md: Test-time compute is not free at serving time. Every extra sample or thinking token is paid on every request, by every user. Training compute is paid once. That asymmetry decides when test-time scaling is worth it.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
md: A TTT layer is an RNN whose hidden state is a model. Update rule = train on the current token. Output rule = predict with the updated model. Choosing the model, the loss and the optimizer chooses the layer.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: After Titans: better objectives, optimal solvers, and replication
md: The successors keep the frame (a memory trained on a key-value loss as the sequence streams) and change what it fits and how well. A window or an exact solve protects earlier writes; a robust loss protects against outliers; forgetting decides how fast a changed fact wins. None of it is settled at scale.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: PEAK and TaHiTI: from backlog to handover
md: Both frameworks end the same way: a hunt is finished when its results are documented and handed to the teams that act on them. The query is not the deliverable. The deliverables are an escalation (if needed), detections, data and security recommendations, and knowledge for the next hunt.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: The intelligence cycle and intelligence requirements
md: The most common failure is a collection-driven programme: buy feeds, read everything, publish a weekly "threat landscape" digest that supports no decision. FIRST warns that a meeting with leadership that is "informational only" will not go well. Start from requirements and work backwards.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Analytic tradecraft: bias and competing hypotheses
md: Weigh evidence by how well it *discriminates* between hypotheses, not by how much of it agrees with your favourite. Look for the item that would disprove each hypothesis, check its sensitivity, and always keep "someone wants us to think this" on the list.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack trees: start from the attacker's goal
md: The numbers are estimates and the tree is never complete. Schneier calls the safe example incomplete and warns not to read its values as a statement about how secure a real safe is. Use trees to compare options and find the cheapest path, not to claim an attack costs exactly 2,200.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance
md: Tiers are not the same as NUMA distance. A remote-socket DRAM node is far, but it has CPUs and DRAM-class performance, so it sits in the top tier and is never a demotion target for the other socket. Only slower memory types form lower tiers.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Prophet, the M4 competition and foundation models
md: Misconception: a bigger or newer model will beat simple methods. On the M4 data pure ML lost to simple combinations, and on our toy series SES with a fitted alpha was no better than naive. Any model, from Prophet to a foundation model, has to beat seasonal naive under rolling-origin evaluation before it ships.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Revocation: CRL, OCSP, stapling, and why short-lived certs won
md: "We revoked the certificate, so we are safe" is wishful thinking. Revocation reaches clients slowly and unreliably. Assume a compromised certificate is usable until it expires, and size your lifetimes accordingly.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
md: Autotuning has costs you do not see in steady state: the first call for each new `key` value compiles and benchmarks every config, and each distinct constexpr combination is a separate compiled kernel. Keep `key` to arguments that really change the best config, and use `prune_configs_by` to drop hopeless candidates.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Evaluating unified models and choosing a design
md: No axis is free. Discrete plus causal is the simplest to train and serve; continuous plus bidirectional plus separate encoders has led the reported GenEval numbers in these papers, at the cost of more moving parts. Pick based on what the product must do well, then evaluate both sides of the model.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Booting on the hypervisor: virtual devices, boot time and memory
md: Do not assume every unikernel does this. Sealing and compile-time randomization are Mirage's design; a 2019 study by the security firm NCC Group of two other unikernels, Rumprun and IncludeOS, found ASLR, W xor X and stack canaries (a random value placed before a function's return address and checked on return, so a buffer overflow is caught) absent or broken.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
md: In graph search the expensive part per hop is often the first touch of a random vector, not the arithmetic. Contiguous fixed-size blocks, aligned vectors, prefetching and smaller (compressed) vectors all attack that same miss.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: One GRPO step through RayPPOTrainer, call by call
md: Read the source, not just the prose. The reward-function doc says the GSM8K scorer (GSM8K, Grade School Math 8K, is OpenAI's set of about 8,500 grade-school math word problems with numeric answers) gives 0.1 for a well-formatted wrong answer, but in the current `gsm8k.py` the default `format_score` is 0.0. A silent difference like that changes what the policy is rewarded for.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: World models, and why Genie learns one from unlabelled video
md: A learned world model is not the real environment. Ha and Schmidhuber found their agent discovered an *adversarial policy* that exploited flaws in M, doing well in the dream but not in reality. They raised a sampling temperature, a knob that scales how random M's samples are (higher means more random), to make the dream noisier and harder to exploit. Every world model in this course shares this risk.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
md: Preprocessing must match the checkpoint. `google/vit-base-patch16-224-in21k` normalizes with mean 0.5 and std 0.5 per channel, while many timm ImageNet models use mean (0.485, 0.456, 0.406). Load the checkpoint's own settings (`AutoImageProcessor` in Transformers, `resolve_data_config` in timm) instead of copying numbers from another model.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Running action chunks in the control loop
md: Temporal ensembling is not a universal upgrade. The pi0 authors tried it early and found it hurt performance, so pi0 executes chunks open-loop: 16 actions then replan on 20 Hz robots (every 0.8 s), 25 actions on 50 Hz robots (every 0.5 s).

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: How vLLM chooses a backend: priority lists and validation
md: Older guides set the `VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND` environment variable. It existed in `vllm/envs.py` up to the v0.14 release and is gone from main. Use `--attention-backend` or `--attention-config` (`-ac`). `AttentionConfig.backend_per_kind` can also set a backend per KV cache group kind, for example a different one for sliding-window MLA layers.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
md: Tiling only helps up to the largest grid the model was trained with. Beyond that the image is downscaled again, and text that was 10 px tall becomes 5 px tall. Check the preprocessing config of the model you deploy, not just the paper.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects
md: Compare&swap is **universal**: an object with consensus number at least $n$ can implement any object wait-free for $n$ processes (next lesson). Fetch&add, swap and test&set are not, so Herlihy proves you cannot build a wait-free compare&swap out of them plus registers for three or more processes.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Rolling a 6-hour step out to 10 days
md: Blurry long-range output from an MSE-trained model is not a bug in the network. It is exactly what MSE asks for under uncertainty. Lesson 5 shows how ensembles and CRPS avoid it.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Recon at bounty scale: wildcards, subdomains and live hosts
md: Recon results are candidates, not permission. A name found in a CT log, a JavaScript file or a scanner's output is tested only if the policy's scope covers it, and never if the policy excludes it.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Reading a programme policy: scope, rules and safe harbour
md: Scope, rules and safe harbour are read together: an in-scope asset tested with a banned method, or with someone else's account, is outside the protection. Safe harbour never extends to third parties the programme does not control.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Cookie attributes: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, Path, prefixes
md: HttpOnly is often oversold. It stops cookie **theft** by script, so an attacker cannot carry the session to their own machine. It does not stop script running in your page from **using** the session right there, which is what the Samy worm did. XSS still needs to be prevented at its source.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: PowerShell: objects in a pipeline, and why attackers like it
md: Misconception: "execution policy stops malicious PowerShell". It does not. Treat it as a seat belt for honest users, and rely on logging, AMSI and application control for security.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WEP: how a 24-bit IV broke Wi-Fi's first encryption
md: A longer WEP key does not help. SP 800-97: the technique "has known flaws that are not mitigated by longer keys". The problems are the tiny IV, the linear checksum and RC4's key schedule, none of which depend on key length. If a device only supports WEP, treat its traffic as unencrypted and isolate it.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Android: UID sandbox, SELinux, verified boot and Play Protect
md: Rooting a phone (gaining root, Unix's all-powerful user) or unlocking its bootloader deliberately removes layers described here: verified boot no longer vouches for the system, and root can override the UID sandbox. Fine for a lab device, a serious risk on one that holds work data; device management and attestation checks such as the Play Integrity API (lesson 16) let organisations detect it.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Production run queues: fixed rings, steal half, a LIFO slot
md: Tokio's local queue is FIFO, not LIFO: the owner pops from the same end thieves steal from. For servers made of many independent tasks, fairness (no task waits forever behind newer ones) matters more than depth-first order. Locality comes from the LIFO slot instead, which Tokio uses at most 3 times in a row to prevent two tasks from starving the queue by waking each other.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
md: Zero-copy means removing the **CPU copies between the page cache, user memory and socket buffers**. Device DMA still happens. The win scales with bytes moved, so it matters when a program mostly shovels data it does not inspect.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Classifying with labels chosen at inference time
md: In a zero-shot classifier, the label text plays the role of the trained weights. Changing a label's wording changes the classifier, so wording, templates, and descriptions are design decisions you test, not decoration.
